content:
Since \(\pi\) maps the finite set \(A=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\) onto itself, \(\pi\) must be a permutation of \(A\). The condition
\[
\pi^6(a)=a \quad \text{for all } a\in A
\]
means \(\pi^6=\mathrm{id}\), so the order of \(\pi\) must divide \(6\).

For a permutation, the order is the least common multiple of its cycle lengths. Therefore, every cycle length must divide \(6\), so the possible cycle lengths are \(1,2,3,6\).

We now list all cycle types of permutations of \(6\) elements using only these cycle lengths, and count each type.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{Cycle type} & \text{Number of permutations} \\
\hline
6 & \dfrac{6!}{6}=120 \\[2mm]
3+3 & \dfrac{6!}{3^2\cdot 2!}=40 \\[2mm]
3+2+1 & \dfrac{6!}{3\cdot 2\cdot 1}=120 \\[2mm]
3+1+1+1 & \dfrac{6!}{3\cdot 3!}=40 \\[2mm]
2+2+2 & \dfrac{6!}{2^3\cdot 3!}=15 \\[2mm]
2+2+1+1 & \dfrac{6!}{2^2\cdot 2!\cdot 2!}=45 \\[2mm]
2+1+1+1+1 & \dfrac{6!}{2\cdot 4!}=15 \\[2mm]
1+1+1+1+1+1 & 1
\end{array}
\]

Adding these counts:
\[
120+40+120+40+15+45+15+1=396.
\]

Thus, the number of such functions is
\[
\boxed{396}.
\]
